vignette: Kofi had always been a driven journalist, but that was before the police brutality he witnessed during a protest two years ago. The event had left him shaken, and the memories still felt more real and vivid than any ordinary memory. When trying to explain what happened, Kofi would often lose his train of thought, unable to finish the story. He would hear the sound of footsteps behind him, like the ones he heard that day, and it would transport him back to the scene. Those footsteps became one of many triggers for Kofi's maladaptive strategies. To avoid being noticed, he started wearing concealing clothing, even in his own neighborhood. He also found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of the event or the friends he had lost during the protest. Certain songs that were popular at the time would bring back memories, and he would quickly change the station. Kofi was aware that these strategies might seem irrational to others, but to him, they felt like necessary precautions. As Kofi's avoidance behaviors intensified, so did his sense of threat. He began to have difficulty concentrating on his work, constantly looking over his shoulder to check if someone was following him. Unfamiliar places became sources of anxiety, as he couldn't assess the danger lurking around every corner. Footsteps behind him would make him jump, and certain songs would send his mind racing back to the traumatic event. Kofi's memories of that day continued to haunt him. The more real they felt, the more he struggled to process them. He became convinced that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him as a journalist and a person. This negative self-appraisal fueled his avoidance behaviors, making it harder for him to engage with the world around him. As Kofi's negative appraisals deepened, so did his sense of threat. He started to see danger everywhere, even in familiar places. His memories of the event became increasingly vivid, and he would find himself reliving them in his mind. The sound of footsteps or certain songs could trigger these memories, sending him spiraling back into a world of fear and anxiety. Kofi's relationship with his partner began to suffer as a result of his maladaptive strategies. His partner would try to encourage him to go out, to engage with the world again, but Kofi was too afraid. He felt like he was losing himself in the process, that the trauma had taken away his happiness and his sense of purpose. Despite his best efforts, Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that his life was no longer his own. The trauma had left him feeling lost and helpless, unable to concentrate or connect with others. His memories of that day continued to haunt him, a constant reminder of what he had lost. As he sat in his darkened apartment, surrounded by the silence and the shadows, Kofi knew he needed help to break free from this cycle of fear and avoidance. It was only when Kofi's editor threatened to fire him due to his lack of productivity that he realized he couldn't keep living like this. He finally sought out therapy, hoping to find a way to overcome his trauma and reclaim his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to manage his triggers, confront his negative appraisals, and rebuild his sense of self.
